newsitem.title: SPAIN: First corruption charge hits Spanish government.
newsitem.headline: First corruption charge hits Spanish government.

text.p: Spain's new conservative government faced its first major crisis on Monday when Defence Minister Eduardo Serra was forced to deny press charges linking him to corruption under the previous Socialist administration.

Serra, an independent who according to local media owes his post to King Juan Carlos, has been in the spotlight for weeks for a reported tug-of-war with Deputy Prime Minister Francisco Alvarez Cascos over control of Spain's intelligence services.
He was also criticised as one of the key movers in the new government's surprise decision to turn down court requests to declassify files on a 1980s "dirty war" on Basque ETA rebels.

The daily El Mundo on Monday quoted court documents as showing that Serra, who had already served as secretary of state for defence under the Socialists, was a top executive of major construction company Cubiertas when it paid more than $1 million in bribes in return for contracts.

Serra denied involvement and said persistent attacks on him by El Mundo might be linked to "something I've done" -- an apparent reference to his role in the cabinet's refusal to declassify the files on the "dirty war" on Basque rebels.
The 1983-87 campaign of bombings, kidnappings, torture and murder killed 27 people, one-third of them by mistake.

"That, the way it is stated, is absolutely false," Serra told a radio interviewer when asked about the corruption report in El Mundo. "Put in those terms, it suggests I took part in that revolting traffic in which I've never been involved in my life, and which I absolutely oppose."
The first official reaction from colleagues in the government came from Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja, who said he trusted Serra's account of events was the right one.
"All we can do is to show him our support and our solidarity," Mayor Oreja told state radio.

Serra said he had been a mere vice-president in Cubiertas y MZOV SA at the time more than $1 million was funnelled to Luis Roldan, a Socialist who was then head of the paramilitary Civil Guard and who is now on trial on a series of embezzlement and corruption charges.
Serra said he was only made president of the company after the scandal blew up and that he was entrusted with the mission of cleaning it up.
But El Mundo, which labelled him "the rotten link" in the government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, said court papers showed the payments had continued after Serra became president.

"If Eduardo Serra wasn't who he is, if he was any other minister in the Aznar government, there is no doubt what his response to the news reported today by El Mundo would be," the paper said in an editorial. "He would resign right away."

Aznar and his centre-right Popular Party took office in May after early elections forced on his Socialist predecessor Felipe Gonzalez by mounting corruption scandals and revelations on the "dirty war" against ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) rebels.
Aznar's campaign relied heavily on the scandals as a weapon against the Socialists and he was sworn in on a clean-hands programme.
El Mundo played a key role in bringing to light Socialist corruption cases and evidence about the illegal anti-ETA campaign under the Socialists.

It has since appeared to split ways with Aznar as the PP performed a full turnaround whether to declassify secret files on the "dirty war", coming to the same conclusion as the Socialists: that the security of the state was at stake.

El Mundo's editor, Pedro Ramirez, wrote a long piece on Sunday blasting Aznar for what he described as the government's inability to understand its own actions and comparing the prime minister to a well-known case in psychiatry: the man who mistook his wife for a hat.
